cards.canonical_statement: For any ordered planar rectangle [a,b], let the vector-field components f,g be continuous on the closed rectangle, with actual derivative fields A,B throughout its open interior. If A(e₁)+B(e₂) is Lebesgue integrable on the rectangle, its area integral equals the outward boundary flux: top minus bottom plus right minus left.
cards.proof_strategy: Use the actual component derivatives to form the divergence.
sketch_steps: Use the actual component derivatives to form the divergence.
Continuity on the closed rectangle includes boundary continuity.
Apply the planar rectangular Gauss theorem with the explicit divergence-integrability premise.
Read the oriented boundary terms as top−bottom+right−left outward flux.

cards.canonical_statement: For any ordered planar rectangle, P,Q continuous on the closed rectangle may fail to have the specified derivatives A,B on a countable exceptional set in the interior. If the scalar curl B(e₁)−A(e₂) is integrable, its area integral equals the counterclockwise circulation of P dx+Q dy around the four sides. No differentiability is asserted on the exceptional set.
cards.proof_strategy: Rotate the field to (Q,−P), whose divergence is the scalar curl.
sketch_steps: Rotate the field to (Q,−P), whose divergence is the scalar curl.
Retain closed-rectangle continuity and exclude only the supplied countable set from the interior derivative hypotheses.
Apply Gauss with countable derivative exceptions and the stated curl-integrability premise.
Negate the horizontal integrals and collect the bottom/right/top/left terms in counterclockwise order.

cards.proof_strategy: Pair the top and bottom integrals, whose x-dependent and constant terms cancel.
sketch_steps: Pair the top and bottom integrals, whose x-dependent and constant terms cancel.
Their difference is δ times the height times the width.
Pair the right and left integrals; their difference is α times the width times the height.
Add the two contributions to obtain the trace coefficient α+δ times signed area.

cards.canonical_statement: If planar f and g are globally C¹, then on every closed bounded rectangle they are continuous, their totalized fderiv fields are actual derivatives at every point, and their divergence is Lebesgue integrable. Thus global C¹ regularity supplies the analytic Gauss hypotheses; endpoint ordering is a separate geometric condition.
cards.proof_strategy: Global C¹ regularity implies continuity on the closed rectangle.
sketch_steps: Global C¹ regularity implies continuity on the closed rectangle.
It also provides actual derivatives everywhere, so fderiv is not being used without a differentiability certificate.
The derivative fields are continuous; evaluating them on fixed coordinate directions and adding preserves continuity.
A continuous divergence is integrable on the compact rectangle.

cards.canonical_statement: For any rectangle with positive width and height and any nonzero c, there exists a scalar component f whose actual derivative is zero at every interior point, yet its right-side flux minus left-side flux is nonzero. Taking the other vector-field component to be zero gives zero interior divergence but nonzero boundary flux: interior differentiability alone cannot replace boundary continuity in Gauss.
cards.proof_strategy: Put f=c on the left boundary line and zero off that line.
sketch_steps: Put f=c on the left boundary line and zero off that line.
Every interior point has a neighborhood disjoint from the left line, so the actual derivative there is zero.
The right-face integral is zero and the left-face integral is c times the positive height.
Their difference is nonzero, giving a general counterexample to dropping boundary continuity.
